slides.heading: Oral Lesson
bullets: In “A man of wealth rode by our house,” look at the little words of and by.
“of” connects wealth to man; “by” connects house to rode.
Each shows how its noun is related to another word in the sentence.
A word used to show such a relation is called a Preposition.

slides.text: A Preposition is a word used to show the relation between its object and some other word.
examples: the noun after it is its object

slides.heading: Common Prepositions
bullets: Place & direction:  in, on, at, by, to, into, from, up, down, over, under.
Others:  of, for, with, without, about, above, below, near, past.
Between things:  between, among, through, across, around, behind, beside.
A preposition almost always sits just before its object (a noun or pronoun).

slides.heading: Practice — Find the Preposition
slides.instruction: Name the preposition (or prepositions) in each sentence.
items: The boy went through the gate.
The light came through the window.
A man of wealth rode by.
Put the book on the shelf.

slides.heading: The Phrase
bullets: A Phrase is a group made of a preposition and its object:  of wealth, by our house.
A phrase does the work of a single adjective or adverb.
Adjective phrase — modifies a noun:  “a man of wealth” tells which man.
Adverbial phrase — modifies a verb:  “rode by our house” tells where he rode.

slides.heading: Practice — Find the Phrase
slides.instruction: Name the prepositional phrase in each sentence.
items: The book on the table is mine.
The dog slept under the porch.

slides.heading: Practice — Adjective or Adverbial Phrase?
slides.instruction: Tell whether the phrase modifies a noun (adjective) or a verb (adverbial).
items: The house on the hill is old.
The man with the hat left.

slides.text: An Infinitive is a form of the verb, usually with “to,” that names an action without asserting it.
examples: To play is pleasant.  (to play = the subject)
He wants to go.  (to go = the object)
John studies to learn.  (to learn tells why)
the word “to” is the sign of the infinitive

slides.heading: The Infinitive at Work
bullets: An infinitive names or points to an action, but does not affirm it.
It can be the subject:  “To lie is wicked.”
It can be the object:  “He wants to go home.”
It can tell why:  “John studies to learn.”
The two parts — “to” and the verb — are kept together.

slides.heading: Practice — Find the Infinitive
slides.instruction: Name the infinitive in each sentence.

slides.heading: Practice — What Is the Infinitive Doing?
slides.instruction: Tell what the infinitive does: is it the subject, the object, or does it tell why?

slides.heading: Where to Put a Modifier
bullets: Place a modifier as near as possible to the word it modifies, or the meaning changes.
“John only studies algebra.” — only John does (no one else).
“John studies algebra only.” — algebra is all he studies.
A misplaced phrase can turn silly:  “A watch was found by a boy with steel hands.”
Keep each word, phrase, and clause beside the word it belongs to.

slides.heading: Practice — What Does It Seem to Say?
slides.instruction: A modifier is out of place, so each sentence says something silly. What does the modifier seem to describe?
items: I saw a man walking a dog with a hat.
She gave a balloon to the kid that was red.
He fed the cat wearing pajamas.
We watched the parade on the roof.
He handed tests to the kids with no names.
I found a wallet walking to school.
What is the object of a preposition?
A phrase that modifies a noun is what kind?
What is the sign of the infinitive?
Where should a modifier be placed?
answers: A word that shows the relation between its object and some other word.
The noun or pronoun that follows it.
A preposition and its object used together.
A verb form, usually with “to,” that names an action without asserting it.
As near as possible to the word it modifies.
